reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because its title and description promote cryptocurrency exchange earnings of up to 1000% per year, while the speaker presents a $100–$200 daily mining income target and solicits recruitment with a 10% return across five generations. The speaker also forecasts continued CRT growth. A sampled mining dashboard separately requests a transfer after a DGB threshold warning, although the recipient, amount, and whether any transfer occurred are not established, and the speaker acknowledges that prices can fall after sharp rises.

citations.quote: EARN on the OneCoin Cryptocurrency Exchange.
you have one bitcoin there but in such case you received 3 bitcoin

from referral system you also earn What your people earned and those whom you invited to start digging, they are your partners, which I want to note paid no rubles to start digging, you get 10 percent for 5 generations

opening.argument: The presentation is framed as conditional market commentary, not a promise of a fixed result. The speaker explicitly acknowledges volatility: after a sharp rise, the trend can fall, and he describes continued growth only as a forecast. Even the income discussion is phrased as an attempt to reach a target, not as an unconditional guarantee. That risk-aware framing matters: viewers are shown examples and predictions about cryptocurrency markets, while the speaker concedes that outcomes depend on price movements and trading decisions.

my prediction is that CRT company will continue to grow
We will try to bring every user with a decent amount of energy in Russia to not lower minimum salary, such as 100-200 dollars a day.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The title and description mention earnings, but they do not establish that every viewer was promised a result. The cited daily figure is qualified by “we will try,” while the speaker expressly discusses prices falling. The referral passage describes a commission structure, but it does not by itself establish that participation required a deposit or that returns were guaranteed.

After a sharp rise There will be. Here is the case that the trend has now fallen.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Risk language does not neutralize the overall earnings solicitation. The description advertises “Investments up to 1000% per year,” and the speaker presents a target of $100–$200 per day. Acknowledging that prices may fall can make a promotion sound balanced without explaining whether users can realistically obtain the advertised outcomes. The referral scheme still links recruitment to income.

opening.argument: The video is most naturally read as an operational demonstration of mining and trading activity. It walks through historical charts, compares acquisition and sale prices, explains switching from one mined currency to another, and discusses how mining software operates while a computer is in use. The speaker presents first-person examples and shows exchange and pool dashboards rather than asking viewers to hand over money. That is consistent with a practical technology and market tutorial: viewers are being shown how the system, charts, mining process, and pool function.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution emphasizes promotional figures, but examples of trading performance and mining operation are still compatible with an educational demonstration. Showing charts and explaining when to run miners does not establish deception. The referral discussion appears late and does not change that most of the material concerns currencies, charts, pool activity, and operational use of computers.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The instructional format does not make the message merely educational. The speaker says users can receive three bitcoin for one bitcoin and describes a daily income target, then gives explicit recruitment commissions. Those are substantive earning appeals, not just neutral explanations of charts or software. Demonstrating a dashboard and mining process supports the promotion rather than separating it from the promotion.

opening.argument: The referral element is described as an ordinary promotional reward attached to users inviting partners, not as proof of a fraudulent investment mechanism. The speaker says those invited to start digging paid no rubles to begin, and describes a percentage earned from what invited people earn. The supplied material does not establish a required deposit, a credential request, or a guaranteed payout, and it does not show that any transfer was completed. Without those additional facts, the evidence supports a mining service with a referral promotion and market commentary, not a demonstrated scam mechanism.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution identifies recruitment commissions, but a commission for referrals is also found in ordinary promotions and does not by itself prove a scam. The cited earnings language does not show a required payment or a guaranteed outcome. The dashboard frame does not establish who would receive a transfer, its amount, or whether one occurred, so it cannot fill that evidentiary gap.

citations.quote: paid no rubles to start digging
you get 10 percent for 5 generations, then 2.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling the arrangement a promotion does not make it ordinary or harmless when the reward is tied to five generations of recruits. The speaker expressly says invited people are partners and that the inviter earns from what they earn. The absence of a shown deposit may distinguish this from one mechanism, but it does not contradict the direct recruitment-income evidence or the surrounding high-return claims.
